hook: This one starts as a dry report about a ruined art piece left out in the Alaskan cold and slowly turns into something much heavier. Read it to the very end, because the closing research note changes how the whole recovery log reads. It is grim in places, but most of that grimness is implied rather than shown.
whyItMatters: It is a featured Keter whose weight comes from people rather than from the object's power. Instead of leaning on mind control as the easy explanation, the final report argues it away, so the article ends up questioning the very idea of a planet that would be better off without us.
thingsToNotice:
Compare the artists' promotional pitch, a gentle contrast between wilderness and decay, with what the globe does once it spins. The detail that the device wears itself down is a neat irony: a machine meant to erase human making cannot escape being human-made.

The recovery log stays clinical while describing a crowd that keeps the last globe turning, and containment now relies on the same northern cold that hurt the survivors. Then Dr. Sorts removes the comfortable explanation. Without a supernatural push, the townspeople's own choice becomes the most disturbing thing in the file.

related.note: Another crowd embracing its own ending, told through dry Foundation records.
A very different machine, built to bring humanity back rather than erase it.
